claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing has revolutionised loss-of-function experiments in Leishmania, the causative agent of leishmaniasis.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing has revolutionised loss-of-function experiments in Leishmania, the causative agent of leishmaniasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of CRISPR/Cas9 technology on Leishmania research, supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: Leishmania lack a functional non-homologous DNA end joining pathway.
source: As Leishmania lack a functional non-homologous DNA end joining pathway however, obtaining null mutants typically requires additional donor DNA, selection of drug resistance-associated edits or time-consuming isolation of clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing Passos-Silva et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2022, which discuss the absence of NHEJ components in Leishmania.

claim: Obtaining null mutants in Leishmania typically requires additional donor DNA, selection of drug resistance-associated edits or time-consuming isolation of clones.
source: As Leishmania lack a functional non-homologous DNA end joining pathway however, obtaining null mutants typically requires additional donor DNA, selection of drug resistance-associated edits or time-consuming isolation of clones.
evidence: This claim is supported by the manuscript's discussion of current limitations in Leishmania gene editing and is referenced in the context of existing CRISPR methods.

claim: Genome-wide loss-of-function screens across different conditions and across multiple Leishmania species are unfeasible at present.
source: Genome-wide loss-of-function screens across different conditions and across multiple Leishmania species are therefore unfeasible at present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations described in the manuscript regarding current CRISPR methods in Leishmania.

claim: The authors employed CBEs in Leishmania to introduce STOP codons by converting cytosine into thymine.
source: We employed CBEs in Leishmania to introduce STOP codons by converting cytosine into thymine and created http://www.leishbaseedit.net/ for CBE primer design in kinetoplastids.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The authors created http://www.leishbaseedit.net/ for CBE primer design in kinetoplastids.
source: We employed CBEs in Leishmania to introduce STOP codons by converting cytosine into thymine and created http://www.leishbaseedit.net/ for CBE primer design in kinetoplastids.
evidence: This is a primary finding and resource developed as part of the study.

claim: The CBE tool can efficiently generate functional null mutants by expressing just one single-guide RNA, reaching up to 100% editing rate in non-clonal populations.
source: Through reporter assays and by targeting single- and multi-copy genes in L. mexicana, L. major, L. donovani, and L. infantum, we demonstrate how this tool can efficiently generate functional null mutants by expressing just one single-guide RNA, reaching up to 100% editing rate in non-clonal populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from reporter assays and gene targeting experiments shown in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: The authors successfully targeted single- and multi-copy genes in L. mexicana, L. major, L. donovani, and L. infantum.
source: Through reporter assays and by targeting single- and multi-copy genes in L. mexicana, L. major, L. donovani, and L. infantum, we demonstrate how this tool can efficiently generate functional null mutants by expressing just one single-guide RNA, reaching up to 100% editing rate in non-clonal populations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4, 5, and 6, showing targeting of PF16, IFT88, MFT, and PFR2 genes.

claim: The authors generated a Leishmania-optimised CBE by replacing the Rad51 ssDBD with a L. major-derived version.
source: We then generated a Leishmania-optimised CBE and successfully targeted an essential gene in a plasmid library delivered loss-of-function screen in L. mexicana.
evidence: This is supported by the description in the Results section and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, showing the construction of hyBE4max-LmajDBD.

claim: The CBE method does not require DNA double-strand breaks, homologous recombination, donor DNA, or isolation of clones.
source: Since our method does not require DNA double-strand breaks, homologous recombination, donor DNA, or isolation of clones, we believe that this enables for the first time functional genetic screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries.
evidence: This is supported by the mechanism of base editing described in the manuscript and the experimental results showing efficient editing without these requirements.

claim: This is the first time functional genetic screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries have been reported.
source: Since our method does not require DNA double-strand breaks, homologous recombination, donor DNA, or isolation of clones, we believe that this enables for the first time functional genetic screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries.
evidence: This is supported by the successful plasmid library screen targeting CRK3 shown in Figure 7.

claim: Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease with poor treatment options, causing an estimated 1 million new cases and 20,000 deaths annually.
source: Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease with poor treatment options, causing an estimated 1 million new cases and 20,000 deaths annually (World-Health-Organization, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2023.

claim: Leishmania species proliferate in sand flies as motile promastigotes and in vertebrates as immotile amastigotes.
source: It is caused by Leishmania species, which proliferate in sand flies as motile promastigotes and in vertebrates as immotile amastigotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Leishmania life cycle.

claim: When injected into a mammalian host, promastigotes predominantly enter macrophages and differentiate inside the phagolysosome into amastigotes.
source: When injected into a mammalian host, promastigotes predominantly enter macrophages (van Zandbergen et al., 2004; Chaves et al., 2020) and differentiate inside the phagolysosome into amastigotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Zandbergen et al., 2004 and Chaves et al., 2020.

claim: Genome-wide RNA interference (RNAi) screens have enabled a detailed functional dissection of nearly all genes in Trypanosoma brucei.
source: While genome-wide RNA interference (RNAi) screens have enabled a detailed functional dissection of nearly all genes in the closely related parasite Trypanosoma brucei (Alsford et al., 2011; Horn, 2022; Morris et al., 2002), this success has not been mirrored in Leishmania.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alsford et al., 2011; Horn, 2022; and Morris et al., 2002.

claim: Only Leishmania species of the Viannia subgenus have retained the components required for RNAi activity.
source: However, only Leishmania species of the Viannia subgenus have retained the components required for RNAi activity, precluding its use as a tool in most other Leishmania parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lye et al., 2010 and Ullu et al., 2004 in the following sentence.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has greatly improved loss-of-function experiments in Leishmania by simplifying previous labour-intensive gene replacement strategies.
source: By simplifying previous labour-intensive gene replacement strategies (Cruz and Beverley, 1990), CRISPR/Cas9 has greatly improved loss-of-function experiments in Leishmania (Beneke et al., 2017; Sollelis et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cruz and Beverley, 1990; Beneke et al., 2017; Sollelis et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2017; and Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015.

claim: The LeishGEdit toolbox has boosted the number of successful loss-of-function studies in Leishmania species.
source: In particular, the introduction of the PCR-based LeishGEdit toolbox (Beneke et al., 2017; Beneke and Gluenz, 2019; Beneke and Gluenz, 2020) has boosted the number of successful loss-of-function studies in Leishmania species (Bryant et al., 2019; Yagoubat et al., 2020a; Jones et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beneke et al., 2017; Beneke and Gluenz, 2019; Beneke and Gluenz, 2020; Bryant et al., 2019; Yagoubat et al., 2020a; and Jones et al., 2018.

claim: LeishGEdit enabled bar-seq screens in which hundreds of barcoded mutants are simultaneously phenotyped by pooling them together.
source: LeishGEdit enabled bar-seq screens in-which hundreds of barcoded mutants are simultaneously phenotyped by pooling them together (Beneke and Gluenz, 2020; Baker et al., 2021; Beneke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beneke and Gluenz, 2020; Baker et al., 2021; and Beneke et al., 2019.

claim: The LeishGEM project attempts to knockout nearly all genes in the Leishmania mexicana genome.
source: Using the LeishGEdit method, the LeishGEM project (http://www.leishgem.org/) attempts to knockout nearly all genes in the Leishmania mexicana genome and plans to uncover key virulence factors by screening barcoded mutants across 170 pooled populations.
evidence: This is a statement about an ongoing project, supported by reference to the LeishGEM website.

claim: Leishmania parasites lack the key components of the non-homologous DNA end joining (NHEJ) pathway, including DNA-PKcs, Ligase IV, and XRCC4.
source: One of the reasons why similar pooled CRISPR transfection screens in Leishmania species have not been performed is that Leishmania parasites, unlike mammalian cells or T. gondii parasites, lack the key components of the non-homologous DNA end joining (NHEJ) pathway, including DNA-PKcs, Ligase IV, and XRCC4 (Passos-Silva et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Passos-Silva et al., 2010 and Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: Following a Cas9-introduced double-strand break, DNA in mammalian cells is mainly repaired by NHEJ (>70% in humans).
source: Following a Cas9-introduced double-strand break (DSB), DNA in mammalian cells and T. gondii parasites is mainly repaired by NHEJ (>70% in humans,>90% in T. gondii of all DSBs), allowing indels and frame-shifts to be efficiently introduced in the target gene (Fenoy et al., 2016; Fox et al., 2009; Gallagher and Haber, 2018; Hsu et al., 2014; Smolarz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fenoy et al., 2016; Fox et al., 2009; Gallagher and Haber, 2018; Hsu et al., 2014; and Smolarz et al., 2014.

claim: Following a Cas9-introduced double-strand break, DNA in T. gondii parasites is mainly repaired by NHEJ (>90% of all DSBs).
source: Following a Cas9-introduced double-strand break (DSB), DNA in mammalian cells and T. gondii parasites is mainly repaired by NHEJ (>70% in humans,>90% in T. gondii of all DSBs), allowing indels and frame-shifts to be efficiently introduced in the target gene (Fenoy et al., 2016; Fox et al., 2009; Gallagher and Haber, 2018; Hsu et al., 2014; Smolarz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fenoy et al., 2016; Fox et al., 2009; Gallagher and Haber, 2018; Hsu et al., 2014; and Smolarz et al., 2014.

claim: Leishmania parasites rely on homologous recombination (HR), single-strand annealing, and microhomology-mediated end joining DNA repair pathways to repair Cas9-introduced DSBs.
source: In contrast, Leishmania parasites rely on homologous recombination (HR), single-strand annealing, and microhomology-mediated end joining DNA repair pathways to repair Cas9-introduced DSBs.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the following sentence to Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015; Zhang et al., 2022; and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Without the addition of repair template DNA, Cas9-introduced DSBs in Leishmania lead to large and unpredictable DNA deletions, increased cell death during DNA repair failures and prolonged repair times.
source: Without the addition of repair template DNA, this leads to large and unpredictable DNA deletions, increased cell death during DNA repair failures and prolonged repair times (Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015; Zhang et al., 2022; and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: CRISPR targeting in Leishmania is highly inefficient and the mutation rate is believed to be less than 1% without addition of donor DNA.
source: In consequence, CRISPR targeting in Leishmania is highly inefficient and the mutation rate is believed to be less than 1% without addition of donor DNA (Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015; Zhang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017; Zhang and Matlashewski, 2015; Zhang et al., 2022; and Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Zhang et al., 2022 attempted to reconstitute the NHEJ pathway of Mycobacterium marinum in Leishmania.
source: Zhang et al., 2022 have recently attempted to reconstitute the NHEJ pathway of Mycobacterium marinum in Leishmania.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: Editing rates in Leishmania remain low without the addition of donor DNA (less than 3% editing in selected non-clonal populations that express Cas9 and one sgRNA) even with reconstituted NHEJ pathway.
source: While the authors claim that this improved DSB repair fidelity and efficiency in Leishmania, editing rates still remain low without the addition of donor DNA (less than 3% editing in selected non-clonal populations that express Cas9 and one sgRNA).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' interpretation of results from Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: CBEs are comprised of a cytidine deaminase domain fused to an impaired form of Cas9.
source: CBEs are comprised of a cytidine deaminase domain fused to an impaired form of Cas9.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CBE structure, supported by citation to Huang et al., 2021 in the following sentence.

claim: The Cas9 module in CBEs provides precise targeting to a site of interest, where the cytidine deaminase can directly convert cytosine to thymine without requiring DSBs, HR, or donor DNA templates.
source: The Cas9 module provides precise targeting of the CBE to a site of interest, where the cytidine deaminase can directly convert cytosine to thymine without requiring DSBs, HR, or donor DNA templates (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2021.

claim: The deaminase domain in CBEs catalyses a deamination reaction, converting cytidine (C) to uridine (U).
source: Specifically, the deaminase domain catalyses a deamination reaction, converting cytidine (C) to uridine (U).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of CBEs.

claim: Uridine is repaired to thymidine (T) during DNA replication.
source: Uridine is then repaired to thymidine (T) during DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of CBEs.

claim: Cas9 nickases (nCas9), such as D10A, are tethered to two monomers of a uracil glycosylase inhibitor (UGI) to prevent base excision repair.
source: To prevent base excision repair, which would convert uridine back to cytidine, Cas9 nickases (nCas9), such as D10A (Cong et al., 2013), are additionally tethered to two monomers of a uracil glycosylase inhibitor (UGI) and further modifications of nuclear localisation signals (NLS), codon usage and the deaminase component have yielded highly efficient editors, such as the BE4max and AncBE4max (Koblan et al., 2018; Komor et al., 2016; Komor et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cong et al., 2013; Koblan et al., 2018; Komor et al., 2016; and Komor et al., 2017.

claim: BE4max and AncBE4max are highly efficient CBE editors.
source: To prevent base excision repair, which would convert uridine back to cytidine, Cas9 nickases (nCas9), such as D10A (Cong et al., 2013), are additionally tethered to two monomers of a uracil glycosylase inhibitor (UGI) and further modifications of nuclear localisation signals (NLS), codon usage and the deaminase component have yielded highly efficient editors, such as the BE4max and AncBE4max (Koblan et al., 2018; Komor et al., 2016; Komor et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koblan et al., 2018; Komor et al., 2016; and Komor et al., 2017.

claim: CBE editing rates can be improved through insertion of a non-sequence-specific single-stranded (ss) DNA-binding domain (DBD) from the Rad51 protein between the Cas9 nickase and the deaminase domain (namely hyBE4max).
source: In addition, CBE editing rates can be further improved through insertion of a non-sequence-specific single-stranded (ss) DNA-binding domain (DBD) from the Rad51 protein between the Cas9 nickase and the deaminase domain (namely hyBE4max) (Figure 1A; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The editing window for hyBE4max is located at positions 4–12 on the PAM sequence containing strand.
source: The editing window is located on the PAM sequence containing strand (yellow) at positions 4–12 (purple).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: One arginine codon can be edited on the coding strand into one STOP codon.
source: While one arginine and two glutamine codons are edited on the coding strand (light blue) into one STOP codon each, the one tryptophan codon on the template strand (dark blue) can be edited into three STOP codons.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Two glutamine codons can be edited on the coding strand into one STOP codon each.
source: While one arginine and two glutamine codons are edited on the coding strand (light blue) into one STOP codon each, the one tryptophan codon on the template strand (dark blue) can be edited into three STOP codons.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: One tryptophan codon on the template strand can be edited into three STOP codons.
source: While one arginine and two glutamine codons are edited on the coding strand (light blue) into one STOP codon each, the one tryptophan codon on the template strand (dark blue) can be edited into three STOP codons.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Suitable single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) that would convert four codons into STOP codons were designed for 64 kinetoplastid species.
source: Suitable single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) that would convert these four codons into STOP codons were designed for 64 kinetoplastid species.
evidence: This is supported by the description in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: On average, at least 2 sgRNAs per gene can be designed for 87.2% of all protein-coding genes in the genomes of 64 kinetoplastids.
source: We could on average design at least 2 sgRNAs per gene for 87.2% of all protein-coding genes in the genomes of 64 kinetoplastids (available through TritrypDB release 59 [Aslett et al., 2010]), including 32 Leishmania species (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: 98.0% of transfected L. major cells had no fluorescent tdTomato signal as early as 11 days post transfection with guide 1 targeting the template strand.
source: For guide 1, targeting the template strand, 98.0% of transfected cells had no fluorescent signal as early as 11 days post transfection ('Target 1' on template strand in Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Guides designed to only introduce neutral substitutions with no amino acid change did not alter the fluorescent signal of the tdTomato reporter even 33 days post transfection.
source: In contrast, guides designed to only introduce neutral substitutions with no amino acid change ('Control' on template and coding strand in Figure 2D), did not alter the fluorescent signal of the reporter even 33 days post transfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The tdTomato reporter cell line showed an increase in doubling time compared to the wildtype cell line (from 5.6 to 7.5 h).
source: While the tdTomato reporter cell line showed an increase in doubling time compared to the wildtype cell line (from 5.6 to 7.5 h), additional transfection of the pLdCH-hyBE4max plasmid did not lead to a further increase in doubling time (Figure 2E), indicating no effect of the editor or guide expression on growth in L. major parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Additional transfection of the pLdCH-hyBE4max plasmid did not lead to a further increase in doubling time in L. major parasites.
source: While the tdTomato reporter cell line showed an increase in doubling time compared to the wildtype cell line (from 5.6 to 7.5 h), additional transfection of the pLdCH-hyBE4max plasmid did not lead to a further increase in doubling time (Figure 2E), indicating no effect of the editor or guide expression on growth in L. major parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Three C to T conversions were 100% effective for 'Target 1' on the template strand at positions 6–8, yielding a STOP codon at the intended position.
source: For example, three C to T conversions were 100% effective for 'Target 1' on the template strand at positions 6–8, yielding a STOP codon at the intended position.
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fourth conversion target of guide 'Target 1' on the template strand at position 12 was not edited.
source: However, the fourth conversion target of that guide at position 12 was not edited (Figure 3A), confirming previously observed differences in editing efficiencies across the editing window (efficiency higher at positions 4–8 than 8–12 [Zhang et al., 2020]).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Both control guides showed high editing rates (100% for Ctrl(+), 79.2% and 45.9% for Ctr(−)) but did not show any changes in the reporter expression.
source: Strikingly, both control guides, which did not show any changes in the reporter expression (Figure 2D) as they were designed to only change the DNA sequence but not the amino acid sequence, showed also high editing rates (100% for Ctrl(+), 79.2% and 45.9% for Ctr(−)), confirming that the hyBE4max CBE was highly specific even though expressed for 33 days (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2D and 3A, B.

claim: The hyBE4max CBE was highly specific even though expressed for 33 days.
source: Strikingly, both control guides, which did not show any changes in the reporter expression (Figure 2D) as they were designed to only change the DNA sequence but not the amino acid sequence, showed also high editing rates (100% for Ctrl(+), 79.2% and 45.9% for Ctr(−)), confirming that the hyBE4max CBE was highly specific even though expressed for 33 days (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that control guides with neutral substitutions did not affect reporter expression despite high editing rates.

claim: Stable expression of hyBE4max increased editing rates, with all six guides reaching nearly 100% editing rate.
source: While the latter strategy increased editing during our tdTomato reporter assay, with all six guides reaching nearly 100% editing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E) and controls showing no effect on the reporter expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), doubling times significantly increased once episomal-expressed sgRNAs were transfected into the cell line expressing constitutively hyBE4max and T7 RNAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Doubling times significantly increased once episomal-expressed sgRNAs were transfected into the cell line expressing constitutively hyBE4max and T7 RNAP.
source: While the latter strategy increased editing during our tdTomato reporter assay, with all six guides reaching nearly 100% editing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–E) and controls showing no effect on the reporter expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), doubling times significantly increased once episomal-expressed sgRNAs were transfected into the cell line expressing constitutively hyBE4max and T7 RNAP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: AncBE4max showed strong editing outside of the guide targeting window.
source: While we observed also high editing rates of 100% for nearly all sgRNAs when targeting tdTomato (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E), we saw strong editing outside of the guide targeting window (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F), depleting the tdTomato reporter signal even in control cells, where only neutral substitutions were intended with no amino acid change (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Editing outside the guide target sequence was not observed when using the hyBE4max CBE.
source: Meanwhile, editing outside the guide target sequence was not observed when using the hyBE4max CBE (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The tdTomato reporter was strongest depleted in L. donovani, followed by L. mexicana, L. infantum, and L. major.
source: While we also achieved full depletion of the tdTomato reporter for selected guides in the other three species, the reporter was strongest depleted in L. donovani, followed by L. mexicana, L. infantum, and L. major (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Expression of the CBE and sgRNA did not affect L. major and L. mexicana growth but it increased significantly doubling times in L. donovani and L. infantum.
source: Expression of the CBE and sgRNA did not affect L. major and L. mexicana growth but it increased significantly doubling times in L. donovani and L. infantum, suggesting that high CBE and sgRNA expression levels may be toxic for these parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: High CBE and sgRNA expression levels may be toxic for L. donovani and L. infantum parasites.
source: Expression of the CBE and sgRNA did not affect L. major and L. mexicana growth but it increased significantly doubling times in L. donovani and L. infantum, suggesting that high CBE and sgRNA expression levels may be toxic for these parasites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed increase in doubling times.

claim: The highest expression of hyBE4max was seen in L. major, followed by L. infantum, L. mexicana, and L. donovani.
source: While protein degradation made an exact quantification of hyBE4max difficult, western blots indicated that the highest expression of hyBE4mas was seen in L. major, followed by L. infantum, L. mexicana, and L. donovani (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Three of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-1, PF16-2, and PF16-3) yielded significantly decreased motility in L. donovani at 14 days post transfection.
source: We measured a significant decrease in motility for three (PF16-1, PF16-2, and PF16-3) of the four guides targeting PF16 in L. donovani at 14 days post transfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In L. mexicana and L. infantum only one guide (PF16-3) yielded a measurable decrease in swimming speed at 14 days post transfection.
source: In L. mexicana and L. infantum only one guide (PF16-3) yielded a measurable decrease in swimming speed, while in L. major no significant effect could be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In L. major no significant effect on swimming speed could be determined at 14 days post transfection for PF16 targeting guides.
source: In L. mexicana and L. infantum only one guide (PF16-3) yielded a measurable decrease in swimming speed, while in L. major no significant effect could be determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: One IFT88 targeting guide (IFT88-1) reduced the swimming speed in the transfected L. infantum population.
source: However, out of the four IFT88 targeting guides, one (IFT88-1) reduced the swimming speed in the transfected L. infantum population (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1) and also yielded the expected flagellar assembly phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1, and microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: IFT88-1 guide yielded the expected flagellar assembly phenotype in L. infantum.
source: However, out of the four IFT88 targeting guides, one (IFT88-1) reduced the swimming speed in the transfected L. infantum population (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1) and also yielded the expected flagellar assembly phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: At 28 days post transfection, three of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-1, PF16-2, and PF16-3) still yielded significantly decreased motility in L. donovani.
source: As expected, we saw for most cell lines a further increase in proportion of cells that showed a decrease in swimming speed when PF16 was targeted. For L. donovani three of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-1, PF16-2, and PF16-3) still yielded significantly decreased motility, while for MFT no significant effect was observed (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: For MFT targeting guides, no significant effect on motility was observed in L. donovani at 28 days post transfection.
source: As expected, we saw for most cell lines a further increase in proportion of cells that showed a decrease in swimming speed when PF16 was targeted. For L. donovani three of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-1, PF16-2, and PF16-3) still yielded significantly decreased motility, while for MFT no significant effect was observed (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In L. mexicana two of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-2 and PF16-3) and one of the PFR2 targeting guides (PFR2-1) showed a significant effect on motility at 28 days post transfection.
source: In L. mexicana two of the four PF16 targeting guides (PF16-2 and PF16-3) and one of the PFR2 targeting guides (PFR2-1) showed now a significant effect (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The percentage of L. infantum cells showing decreased mutant speed was lower for the IFT88 targeting guide (IFT88-1) at 28 days post transfection.
source: In L. infantum, the percentage of cells showing decreased mutant speed was now lower for the IFT88 targeting guide (IFT88-1), which is expected as the deletion of IFT88 in L. mexicana has been shown to reduce the doubling time (Beneke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1, and citation to Beneke et al., 2019.

claim: L. infantum parasites with a deleterious IFT88 mutation are most likely outcompeted from the mutant population.
source: L. infantum parasites with a deleterious IFT88 mutation are therefore most likely outcompeted from the mutant population (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in cells with motility phenotype over time.

claim: At 42 days post transfection, L. major parasites transfected with PF16-3 guide showed cells with a motility phenotype.
source: For L. major parasites, we finally could detect cells with a motility phenotype within the PF16 guide transfected population (PF16-3).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The transfected IFT88 guide (IFT88-1) did not induce any measurable effect in L. major at 42 days post transfection.
source: However, the transfected IFT88 guide (IFT88-1) still did not induce any measurable effect in L. major (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis data shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Observed motility phenotypes correlated well with editing rates.
source: Observed motility phenotypes correlated well with editing rates.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of motility data in Figure 4 with editing rate data in Figure 5.

claim: Guide PF16-3 showed high editing rates in all four species with up to 100% C to T conversion.
source: For example, guide PF16-3, yielding the strongest decrease in motility across all species, showed high editing rates in all four species with up to 100% C to T conversion.
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Guide PF16-2 only showed editing in L. mexicana and L. donovani.
source: Guide PF16-2, which only showed a motility phenotype in L. mexicana and L. donovani, also only showed editing in those two species and guide PF16-1, which only showed a decrease in mutant speed in L. donovani, also just showed editing in L. donovani (Figures 4B and 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and motility data in Figure 4B.

claim: Guide PF16-1 only showed editing in L. donovani.
source: Guide PF16-2, which only showed a motility phenotype in L. mexicana and L. donovani, also only showed editing in those two species and guide PF16-1, which only showed a decrease in mutant speed in L. donovani, also just showed editing in L. donovani (Figures 4B and 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5A and motility data in Figure 4B.

claim: High editing rates were observed for three of the four IFT88 targeting guides in L. infantum and L. major but only guide IFT88-1 resulted in a measurable motility and flagellar assembly phenotype in L. infantum.
source: Surprisingly, we saw high editing rates for three of the four IFT88 targeting guides in L. infantum and L. major but only guide IFT88-1 resulted in a measurable motility and flagellar assembly phenotype in L. infantum (Figures 4B and 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5B, motility data in Figure 4B, and microscopy data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only guide IFT88-1 induced a mutation that resulted in a STOP codon, while non-STOP codon mutations became dominant for the other two guides.
source: Analysing the Sanger sequencing trace plots further, we noticed that only guide IFT88-1 induced a mutation that resulted in a STOP codon, while non-STOP codon mutations became dominant for the other two guides (Supplementary file 2), presumably due to the known IFT88 growth phenotype (Beneke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data in Supplementary file 2 and citation to Beneke et al., 2019.

claim: For guides targeting PFR2 in L. mexicana, only guide PFR2-1 was efficient.
source: For guides targeting PFR2 in L. mexicana, only guide PFR2-1 was efficient, which was also the only guide resulting in decreased motility (Figures 4B and 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5C and motility data in Figure 4B.

claim: Guide PFR2-1 resulted in a strong knockdown of PFR2 protein (~97% knockdown compared to wildtype).
source: To confirm that indeed, the knockdown of PFR2 was successful, we analysed the expression of the targeted protein by western blot, confirming a strong knockdown only for guide PFR2-1 (~97% knockdown compared to wildtype) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: This strong knockdown of PFR2 was achieved in non-clonal populations that had been selected to express the hyBE4max and only one sgRNA.
source: It is important to highlight that this strong knockdown was achieved in non-clonal populations that had been selected to express the hyBE4max and only one sgRNA.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design described in the manuscript.

claim: PFR2 is a three-copy gene in a tandem array.
source: This is despite the fact that PFR2 is a three-copy gene in a tandem array.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PFR2 gene structure in Leishmania.

claim: Parasites transfected with pLdCH-hyBE4max plasmids that allowed to express MFT targeting guides became significantly resistant to high doses of miltefosine (50 and 80 µM).
source: Pre-treated with miltefosine or not, wildtype cells were only resistant to small doses of miltefosine (5 and 20 µM). In comparison, parasites transfected with pLdCH-hyBE4max plasmids that allowed to express MFT targeting guides became significantly resistant to high doses of miltefosine (50 and 80 µM) (guide MFT-1 and MFT-3 significantly different in Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When pre-treated with miltefosine, the proportion of viable parasites at high miltefosine concentrations rose further and three out of four guides were able to confer resistance (guide MFT-1, MFT-2, and MFT-3).
source: As expected, when pre-treated with miltefosine the proportion of viable parasites at high miltefosine concentrations then rose further and three out of four guides were able to confer resistance (guide MFT-1, MFT-2, and MFT-3 significantly different in Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Viability rates correlated well with high editing rates for MFT targeting guides.
source: In addition, viability rates correlated well with high editing rates for all these three guides.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of viability data in Figure 6B, C with editing rate data in Figure 6D, E.

claim: Guide MFT-3 resulted in the highest editing rate of all MFT targeting guides (up to 81.9% for non-pre-treated cells and 86.5% for pre-treated cells).
source: For example, guide MFT-3, which conferred the highest level of resistance to miltefosine (Figure 6B, C), resulted also in the highest editing rate of all MFT targeting guides (up to 81.9% for non-pre-treated cells and 86.5% for pre-treated cells) (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 6D, E.

claim: The introduced mutations in MFT resulted in the intended premature STOP codon.
source: Further analysis of trace plots also highlighted that the introduced mutations resulted in the intended premature STOP codon (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The CBE method can potentially be used for positive and antileishmanial drug-resistant screening.
source: This demonstrates that our method can potentially be used for positive and antileishmanial drug-resistant screening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful miltefosine resistance screening shown in Figure 6.

claim: Out of all 26 guides used in this study, 24 guides resulted in editing exclusively within the expected hyBE4max 4–12 editing window.
source: Out of all 26 guides used in this study, including tdTomato targeting guides from above, 24 guides resulted in editing exclusively within the expected hyBE4max 4–12 editing window (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of Sanger sequencing data across all experiments and citation to Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: One guide showed editing activity within 3nt range of the 4–12 editing window (tdTomato guide Target 2 (+)).
source: One guide showed editing activity within 3nt range of the 4–12 editing window (tdTomato guide Target 2 (+); Figure 3A) and one guide resulted in editing within 6nt range of the guide sequence (PF16-1 in L. donovani; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: One guide resulted in editing within 6nt range of the guide sequence (PF16-1 in L. donovani).
source: One guide showed editing activity within 3nt range of the 4–12 editing window (tdTomato guide Target 2 (+); Figure 3A) and one guide resulted in editing within 6nt range of the guide sequence (PF16-1 in L. donovani; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Editing rates of guides showing editing outside the 4–12 window were relatively low (23% and 25–27%, respectively), while editing within the 4–12 editing window reached up to 100%.
source: However, editing rates of these two guides were relatively low (23% and 25–27%, respectively), while editing within the 4–12 editing window reached up to 100%.
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data analysis.

claim: The Leishmania version of Rad51 ssDBD contains an N-terminal extension that is bound to the conserved Rad51 ssDBD part through a glutamine-rich repeat.
source: Comparing the Rad51 ssDBD from Leishmania with the human version, the Leishmania version contains an N-terminal extension that is bound to the conserved Rad51 ssDBD part through a glutamine-rich repeat (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glutamine-rich repeats can increase DNA–protein binding by forming hydrogen bonds via their amide site chains.
source: Glutamine-rich repeats, known to be enriched in transcription factors, can increase DNA–protein binding by forming hydrogen bonds via their amide site chains (Perutz et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perutz et al., 1994.

claim: L. major had the longest glutamine-rich repeat among the tested Leishmania species.
source: Since L. major had the longest glutamine-rich repeat among our tested Leishmania species, we decided to replace the Rad51 ssDBD in pLdCH-hyBE4max with an L. major-derived Rad51 ssDBD, giving rise to pLdCH-hyBE4max-LmajDBD (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Leishmania-optimised CBE version showed an increase in the knockdown effect for two of the four targeting guides at 16 days post transfection (1.6-fold increase for guide Target 2 on the coding strand and 5.3-fold increase for guide Target 2 on the template strand).
source: First, we repeated our tdTomato reporter assay and saw an increase in the knockdown effect for the Leishmania-optimised CBE version for two of the four targeting guides at 16 days post transfection (1.6-fold increase for guide Target 2 on the coding strand and 5.3-fold increase for guide Target 2 on the template strand).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For all other guides, including control guides, no major difference between both CBE versions could be detected.
source: For all other guides, including control guides that were designed not to yield a STOP codon, no major difference between both CBE versions could be detected (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The viability phenotype of an essential gene could be detected in a pooled screening format.
source: Therefore, our assumption was that the viability phenotype of an essential gene could especially be detected in a pooled screening format.
evidence: This is speculation based on the expected behavior of essential gene mutations in pooled populations.

claim: An average representation of ~15 transfectants/guide was achieved in the library screen.
source: This showed an average representation of ~15 transfectants/guide (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), which is three times as high as typically used in pooled RNAi libraries in T. brucei (Morris et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and citation to Morris et al., 2002.

claim: Most transfectants had just been transfected with a single episome.
source: This showed that most transfectants had just been transfected with a single episome.
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Three out of eight sequenced clones maintained two different plasmids and by that expressed two sgRNAs.
source: However, three out of eight sequenced clones maintained two different plasmids and by that expressed two sgRNAs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Two of the four CRK3 targeting guides (CRK3-3 and CRK3-4) were significantly depleted at days 12 and 21 in the Leishmania-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max-LmajDBD).
source: Strikingly, we found two of the four CRK3 targeting guides (CRK3-3 and CRK3-4) to be significantly depleted at days 12 and 21 in the Leishmania-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max-LmajDBD), while only one CRK3 guide (CRK3-3) was significant depleted from the non-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max).
evidence: This claim is supported by Illumina sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Only one CRK3 guide (CRK3-3) was significantly depleted from the non-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max).
source: Strikingly, we found two of the four CRK3 targeting guides (CRK3-3 and CRK3-4) to be significantly depleted at days 12 and 21 in the Leishmania-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max-LmajDBD), while only one CRK3 guide (CRK3-3) was significant depleted from the non-optimised CBE library (pLdCH-hyBE4max).
evidence: This claim is supported by Illumina sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: All other guides, including non-targeting guides, did not significantly change in their representation within the pool over time.
source: All other guides, including non-targeting guides, did not significantly change in their representation within the pool over time (Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Illumina sequencing data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The CBE method can be used to target essential genes in pooled transfections.
source: This demonstrates that our method can not only be used to target essential genes but also to pursue loss-of-function screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries.
evidence: This is supported by the successful targeting of CRK3, an essential gene, in the plasmid library screen shown in Figure 7.

claim: The CBE method can be used to pursue loss-of-function screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries.
source: This demonstrates that our method can not only be used to target essential genes but also to pursue loss-of-function screens in Leishmania via delivery of plasmid libraries.
evidence: This is supported by the successful plasmid library screen shown in Figure 7.

claim: This is the first time a plasmid library transfection loss-of-function screen has been reported in Leishmania.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time a plasmid library transfection loss-of-function screen has been reported in Leishmania, enabling large-scale screens under various conditions in multiple Leishmania species in the future.
evidence: This is supported by the successful plasmid library screen shown in Figure 7 and the lack of prior reports of such screens in Leishmania.

claim: The base editing efficacy was shown to be time dependent and to vary widely amongst genes, species, and chosen sgRNA sequences.
source: On the contrary, the base editing efficacy was here also shown to be time dependent and to vary widely amongst genes, species, and chosen sgRNA sequences.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown throughout the manuscript, particularly in Figures 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Variations in efficacy across sgRNAs that target the same gene and locus are a common problem in any CRISPR approach, including CRISPR bar-seq screens.
source: This is not surprising, especially as variations in efficacy across sgRNAs that target the same gene and locus are a common problem in any CRISPR approach, including CRISPR bar-seq screens (Labuhn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Labuhn et al., 2018.

claim: By base editing produced knockdowns are technically truncations and open reading frames (ORFs) are not fully replaced.
source: It is also worth highlighting that by base editing produced knockdowns are technically truncations and open reading frames (ORFs) are not fully replaced.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the base editing mechanism described in the manuscript.

claim: It is unclear whether mutant mRNAs harbouring truncated ORFs have any additional effects on the parasites or whether they are quickly degraded.
source: It is unknown whether mutant mRNAs harbouring these truncated ORFs have any additional effects on the parasites or whether they are quickly degraded.
evidence: This is speculation about the fate of mutant mRNAs.

claim: It is unclear whether a classical nonsense-mediated decay pathway is functional in Leishmania and other kinetoplastids.
source: Degradation of mutant mRNAs in which a termination codon is present within the ORF would require a classical nonsense-mediated decay pathway. But it is unclear whether this pathway is functional in Leishmania and other kinetoplastids (Clayton, 2019; Delhi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clayton, 2019 and Delhi et al., 2011.

claim: Remaining N-terminal protein parts could be functional or even deleterious themselves, leading to false positive and negative results.
source: Thus remaining N-terminal protein parts could be functional or even deleterious themselves, leading to false positive and negative results.
evidence: This is speculation about potential effects of truncated proteins.

claim: The CBE tool can be used to pursue targeted mutagenesis screens.
source: However, this may also provide extra information about functional domains of the targeted protein and highlights that our tool can not only be used to create functional null mutants by inserting premature STOP codons but also to pursue targeted mutagenesis screens.
evidence: This is an inference based on the potential to study truncated proteins.

claim: ssDNA oligo pools can be obtained commercially and used to generate sgRNA libraries.
source: To facilitate large-scale base editing CRISPR screens, ssDNA oligo pools can be obtained commercially and used to generate sgRNA libraries.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRISPR library generation.

claim: The generation of CRISPR libraries is straight forward and scalable, with some libraries containing as many as ~215,000 sgRNAs.
source: The generation of CRISPR libraries is straight forward and scalable, with some libraries containing as many as ~215,000 sgRNAs (Horlbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Horlbeck et al., 2016.

claim: Guides in CRISPR libraries are designed to be gene specific and have a much greater specificity than RNAi plasmid libraries that are typically comprised of randomly sheared genomic DNA.
source: Guides are designed to be gene specific and have therefore a much greater specificity than RNAi plasmid libraries that are typically comprised of randomly sheared genomic DNA, such as those previously used for T. brucei (Alsford et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alsford et al., 2011 and Morris et al., 2002.

claim: The base editing method could be scaled up to facilitate genome-wide screens in future studies.
source: Since the vector we here use for base editing is compatible with this cloning strategy, we believe that our base editing method could be scaled up to facilitate genome-wide screens in future studies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the compatibility of the vector with standard CRISPR library cloning strategies.

claim: Prolonged guide targeting may cause unwanted side effects, such as off-target mutations.
source: What remains to be improved however, is the long culture time needed for some guides in order to reach high C to T conversion rates because prolonged guide targeting may cause unwanted side effects, such as off-target mutations (Grünewald et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grünewald et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: Apart from one guide (PF16-1 in L. donovani), editing outside of the 20nt guide sequence was not detected even 33 days post transfection when analysing the entire Sanger sequencing range of all targeted genes.
source: However, apart from one guide (PF16-1 in L. donovani; Supplementary file 2), which resulted in editing within 6nt range of the guide sequence, we did not detect any editing outside of the 20nt guide sequence even 33 days post transfection when analysing the entire Sanger sequencing range of all our targeted genes (Figures 3A, B, 5A–C,, 6D, E and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figures 3A, B, 5A–C, 6D, E and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Editing time could be reduced by fine-tuning sgRNA and CBE expression, especially through the use of species-specific promoters, synthetic promoters, modified T7 RNAP promoters and stable integration of expression constructs.
source: Editing time could be reduced by fine-tuning sgRNA and CBE expression, especially through the use of species-specific promoters, synthetic promoters, modified T7 RNAP promoters and stable integration of expression constructs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the method.

claim: Integrating sgRNA constructs would ensure that sgRNAs are not lost during in vivo screening and that just one sgRNA per transfectant is expressed.
source: Integrating sgRNA constructs would also ensure that sgRNAs are not lost during in vivo screening and that just one sgRNA per transfectant is expressed, thereby reducing the risk of horizontal plasmid transfer between parasites throughout a screen.
evidence: This is speculation about potential benefits of integrating sgRNA constructs.

claim: It may be preferable to target the template strand (−) over the coding strand (+) to reduce editing time.
source: To reduce editing time, it may be also preferable to target the template strand (−) over the coding strand (+).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that targeting the coding strand leads to slower editing.

claim: Mutations on the coding strand have no immediate effect on the transcript and first need to be incorporated on the template strand (−) during DNA replication.
source: Since mutations on the coding strand have no immediate effect on the transcript, they first need to be incorporated on the template strand (−) during DNA replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of base editing.

claim: Targeting the coding strand leads to a slower increase in editing over time.
source: Hence, targeting the coding strand leads to a slower increase in editing over time and this was also repeatedly reflected in our data (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The guide ranking on the primer design platform has been adjusted to prioritize guides targeting the template strand.
source: We therefore have adjusted our scoring criteria for ranking guides on our primer design platform http://www.leishbaseedit.net/.
evidence: This is a methodological improvement made by the authors.

claim: Guides with fewer cytosine bases within the editing window would result in higher rates of successful STOP codon transformations.
source: Although we have not measured this yet, the expectation would be that guides with fewer cytosine bases within the editing window would result in higher rates of successful STOP codon transformations.
evidence: This is speculation about potential guide design improvements.

claim: Modifying the CBE version through codon optimisation, addition of species-specific NLS or exchange of deaminase and UGI domains, could further increase the editing rate in Leishmania.
source: Lastly, modifying the CBE version through codon optimisation, addition of species-specific NLS or exchange of deaminase and UGI domains, could further increase the editing rate in Leishmania.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the CBE.

claim: The Leishmania-optimised hyBE4max CBE version increases the editing efficiency.
source: We show that our Leishmania-optimised hyBE4max CBE version increases the editing efficiency (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: It remains to be explored whether fidelity and editing window size is affected by the Leishmania-optimised CBE modification.
source: However, it remains to be explored whether also fidelity and editing window size is affected by this modification, as for example hyBE4max adaptations in rise are known to have expanded the editing windows (Wei et al., 2022).
evidence: This is speculation about potential effects of the modification, supported by citation to Wei et al., 2022.

claim: The improved CBE version allowed to efficiently induce a knockdown of CRK3.
source: While especially our improved CBE version allowed to efficiently induce a knockdown of CRK3, guides targeting IFT88 were not significantly depleted in our small-scale library screen (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Guides targeting IFT88 were not significantly depleted in the small-scale library screen.
source: While especially our improved CBE version allowed to efficiently induce a knockdown of CRK3, guides targeting IFT88 were not significantly depleted in our small-scale library screen (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: IFT88 is not an essential gene but is required for normal promastigote proliferation.
source: Although IFT88 is not an essential gene, we would have also expected a decrease in guide abundance over time as IFT88 has been shown to be required for normal promastigote proliferation (Beneke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Beneke et al., 2019.

claim: Universal sgRNAs were prioritized over the highest scoring guides to target IFT88 in multiple species in this study.
source: It is important to note that we prioritised universal sgRNAs over the highest scoring guides to target IFT88 in multiple species in this study.
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors.

claim: By picking higher scoring guides, a depletion of IFT88 guides from the pool could have been achieved.
source: It is therefore possible that by picking higher scoring guides, a depletion of IFT88 guides from the pool could have been achieved.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to guide selection.

claim: Through base editing produced knockdowns are technically truncations with remaining N-terminal protein parts that could be functional.
source: It is also worth highlighting again that through base editing produced knockdowns are technically truncations with remaining N-terminal protein parts that could be functional.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the base editing mechanism and speculation about potential protein function.

claim: The exact timing of isolating DNA from pools might influence when a decrease of parasites with a deleterious mutation is detectable.
source: In addition, the exact timing of isolating DNA from pools might influence when a decrease of parasites with a deleterious mutation is detectable.
evidence: This is speculation about experimental design considerations.

claim: To detect the whole range of mutant phenotypes, a tighter collection window of isolating DNA from pools may be needed.
source: Thus, to detect the whole range of mutant phenotypes, such as IFT88, a tighter collection window of isolating DNA from pools may be needed.
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements to the screening protocol.

claim: Cells with an introduced premature STOP codon in an essential gene can be significantly depleted from a library with the CBE approach.
source: Nevertheless, we demonstrate through targeting of CRK3 that cells with an introduced premature STOP codon in an essential gene can be significantly depleted from a library with our approach (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A functional dissection of the vast majority of Leishmania genes remains to be performed.
source: To date, a functional dissection of the vast majority of Leishmania genes remains to be performed and a lack of suitable tools limits the ability of the field to pursue large-scale loss-of-function screens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of Leishmania research.

claim: A lack of suitable tools limits the ability of the field to pursue large-scale loss-of-function screens in Leishmania.
source: To date, a functional dissection of the vast majority of Leishmania genes remains to be performed and a lack of suitable tools limits the ability of the field to pursue large-scale loss-of-function screens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of Leishmania research.

claim: LeishBASEedit allows to efficiently transform codons into STOP codons, thereby enabling the functional disruption of single- and multi-copy genes without requiring DSBs, HR, donor DNA, or isolation of clones.
source: Here, we report a CRISPR/Cas9 CBE toolbox for Leishmania that fulfils these criteria. LeishBASEedit allows to efficiently transform codons into STOP codons, thereby enabling the functional disruption of single- and multi-copy genes without requiring DSBs, HR, donor DNA, or isolation of clones.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CBE tool can be used for drug resistance screening.
source: We demonstrate that this tool can be used for drug resistance screening, to target essential genes and to pursue loss-of-function screens in a pooled plasmid library transfection format.
evidence: This claim is supported by the miltefosine resistance screening shown in Figure 6.

claim: The CBE method will enable large-scale loss-of-function screens in Leishmania in many laboratories around the globe, simply by just sharing plasmid libraries.
source: We therefore believe that this method will enable large-scale loss-of-function screens in Leishmania in many laboratories around the globe, simply by just sharing plasmid libraries.
evidence: This is speculation about the future impact of the method.

claim: The CBE method will potentially allow for genome-wide screens under different conditions in various clinical isolates and across multiple Leishmania species without limitations due to extreme cases of gene copy numbers and/or aneuploidy or lack of RNAi components.
source: This will potentially even allow for genome-wide screens under different conditions in various clinical isolates and across multiple Leishmania species without limitations due to extreme cases of gene copy numbers and/or aneuploidy or lack of RNAi components.
evidence: This is speculation about the future applications of the method.
